pick up the non-linear correlation between $m_{0}(X)$ and the non-linear
part of $p(X)$.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way.

A. Only Case 1

4.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, 
$\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ unconfoundedness conditional
on $X$ is

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,  $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

Case 1.  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  Then

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$

the ordinary difference in means is the ATE and is $>0$ a.s.

Case 2.  $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but the regression is $Y\sim1+D$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The first term is $>0$ but $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is the
selection on $X$ and can be made arbitrarily negative.  E.g.
$X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ though $\tau>0$ a.s.  The marginal OLS
slope $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ is not sign guaranteed.

Case 3.  Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$.
Put $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ for the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and
$r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, so $E[r(X)]=E[Xr(X)]=0$.
Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)
+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$

and $ \beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$.
The first term $E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial
effect $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$.  With the linear residual the second term
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under the stated non-parametric
assumptions.  $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of the propensity, orthogonal
only to $1,X$.  With $p(x)$ non-linear in $X$ we can take
$m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$ small.
Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau_{0}>0$ for every $x$ but
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau_{0}p(1-p)]-K\,E[r^{2}]<0$, i.e.
$\beta_{D|X}<0$.

Hence positivity of the non-parametric partial effect
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ holds, but the linear
projection $D-a-bX$ is not $D-E[D|X]$ under no functional form
assumptions.  The sign of the population OLS coefficient on $D$ is
forced only by unconditional randomisation.

Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive. A. Only Case 1

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the consensus on Cases 1 and 2 is right, and it points to Case 3 being positive as well.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$, so $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]>0$ and the OLS slope is the ATE.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson problem. With $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$,
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is selection on $X$. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_0(x)$ it can dominate the positive $E[\tau(X)|D=1]$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s. So the unadjusted regression need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is actually in the regression. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[Y_1-Y_0|X]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ in $L^2$, i.e. the linear residual from projecting $D$ on $X$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=E[Y D|X]-E[D|X]E[Y|X]=m_0(X)E[\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
Because $E[\tilde D|X]=E[D|X]-a-bX$ has mean zero and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, the $m_0(X)$ term is mean independent of the $X$-orthogonal component of $D$ and
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)$ up to the linear projection of $p(X)$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}>0$
and $Var(\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}>0$.
In population the Frisch-Waugh coefficient
$\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$
is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ contrasts $\tau(X)>0$. The linear control for $X$ removes the $m_0(X)$ selection that drives Case 2, and the remaining variation in $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation, so it is positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$.

That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: once you partial out $X$, the treated and controls are comparable at each $x$ and the partial association inherits the within-$x$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$. The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and the linear residual $\tilde D$ is the population $L^2$ analogue used by OLS; under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ it preserves the sign.

So positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1, and also by conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled in Case 3, but not for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

5.text:
The potential outcomes can be written as $Y=Y_{0}+D\,\tau$ with $\tau>0$ a.s.
Put $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$ and $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$.
Under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X=x,D=d]=m_{0}(x)+d\,\tau(x)$ ,  
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$.

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The simple OLS slope is the ATE and is strictly positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The first term is $>0$ but the selection term can be made arbitrarily
negative.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$,
$p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.
Hence the marginal difference in means, i.e. the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$, is
not sign guaranteed.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $Y$ is linearly projected on $1,D,X$.
Let $D_{\perp}=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and 
$r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[D_{\perp}|X]$. Then

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})
=E\big[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\big]+E\big[r(X)\{m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)\}\big]
>0+{\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.

The first term is $>0$. The second term is $\operatorname{Cov}(E[Y|X],r)$.
$r$ is the non-linear part of the propensity. With no functional form
condition on $m_{0}(\cdot)$ we can make $E[r(X)m_{0}(X)]$ arbitrarily
negative, e.g. $m_{0}(x)=-k\,r(x)$ with $k$ large and $\tau(x)>0$
small. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})<0$ and

$\beta_{D|X}= \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})/\operatorname{Var}(D_{\perp})<0$

even though $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.
Positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, but not for
the linear residual $D-a-bX$.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced
only by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed the
wrong way by an $X$-dependent propensity and by non-linearity of
$E[Y_{0}|X]$.

A. Only Case 1

6.text:
The population coefficient is the linear projection of $Y$ on the design matrix.

Put $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$,
$p(X)=E[D|X]$ and under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,  $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The simple mean difference is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but the regression is $Y=\alpha+\beta D+u$.

$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$

The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is free. With
$p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate the positive first term.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$
gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $\tau>0$ a.s. The
marginal OLS slope is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ and need not be $>0$.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual
of $D$ on $1,X$ and $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)
&=E\!\left[\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D|X)\right]
   +\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\right)\\
&=E\!\left[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)\right]
   +\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\right)\\
&=E\!\left[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))\right]
   +\operatorname{Cov}\!\bigl(m_{0}(X),r(X)\bigr)
   +\operatorname{Cov}\!\bigl(p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first term is $>0$. The first covariance term is unrestricted under
the stated non-parametric assumptions. If $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear in $X$
$r(X)\not\equiv0$. Choose $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)>0$
small. Then $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$ but
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and $\beta_{D|X}=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)<0$.

Positivity
$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(Y,D-E[D|X]\right)=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$
holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the linear
residual $D-a-bX$. Linear control for $X$ does not absorb the non-linear
part of $m_{0}(X)$ relative to the non-linear part of $p(X)$.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced
only by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either
way with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

A. Only Case 1.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are close to consensus on the first two cases and that the debate is really about Case 3.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s., so the simple OLS slope is the ATE and must be $>0$.

Case 2 with $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but no $X$ in the regression is not guaranteed. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$,
and $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ fall where $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ is high, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$. The marginal OLS can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. So Case 2 is not forced.

Case 3 is conditional randomisation with $X$ in the linear projection. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)>0$ a.s., so $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.

Write the Frisch-Waugh residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=E[m_{0}(X)\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
Because $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX$ has mean zero and $E[Y_{0}|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]$, the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is uncorrelated with the part of $D$ that is orthogonal to $1,X$, and
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)$ up to the linear projection of $p(X)$ on $1,X$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\!\big(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\big)$ 
and the second term is removed by the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$. The remaining term is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D|X)>0$, so $Cov(Y,\tilde D)>0$ and $Var(\tilde D)>0$.

In words, after projecting out the linear part of $D$ that is explained by $X$, the residual part of $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation and is positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: conditioning on $X$, treated and controls are comparable at each $x$, and the linear control for $X$ delivers that comparability in $L^{2}$.

The $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ construction that makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ requires baseline income to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity and it needs $\tau$ to be taken arbitrarily small to be dominated. That is a knife-edge alignment of $m_{0}(\cdot)$ with the non-linear component of $p(\cdot)$ that is not a generic consequence of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions the within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is preserved by the linear partial association.

So positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation, Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$

I think the consensus on Cases 1 and 2 is right, and it points to Case 3 being positive as well.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation: $D\perp Y_0,Y_1$, so $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]>0$ and the OLS slope is the ATE.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson problem. With $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$,
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The second term is selection on $X$. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_0(x)$ it can dominate the positive $E[\tau(X)|D=1]$, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_1>Y_0$ a.s. So the unadjusted regression need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is actually in the regression. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[Y_1-Y_0|X]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ in $L^2$, i.e. the linear residual from projecting $D$ on $X$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=E[Y D|X]-E[D|X]E[Y|X]=m_0(X)E[\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
Because $E[\tilde D|X]=E[D|X]-a-bX$ has mean zero and $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$, the $m_0(X)$ term is mean independent of the $X$-orthogonal component of $D$ and
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)$ up to the linear projection of $p(X)$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}>0$
and $Var(\tilde D)=E[Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}>0$.
In population the Frisch-Waugh coefficient
$\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$
is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ contrasts $\tau(X)>0$. The linear control for $X$ removes the $m_0(X)$ selection that drives Case 2, and the remaining variation in $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation, so it is positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$.

That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: once you partial out $X$, the treated and controls are comparable at each $x$ and the partial association inherits the within-$x$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$. The non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ gives $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and the linear residual $\tilde D$ is the population $L^2$ analogue used by OLS; under $D\perp Y_0,Y_1|X$ it preserves the sign.

So positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1, and also by conditional randomisation once $X$ is controlled in Case 3, but not for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2.

That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I think we are close to consensus on the first two cases and that the debate is really about Case 3.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s., so the simple OLS slope is the ATE and must be $>0$.

Case 2 with $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but no $X$ in the regression is not guaranteed. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$,
and $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ can be made arbitrarily negative by letting $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ fall where $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ is high, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$. The marginal OLS can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. So Case 2 is not forced.

Case 3 is conditional randomisation with $X$ in the linear projection. Under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)>0$ a.s., so $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.

Write the Frisch-Waugh residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=E[m_{0}(X)\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
Because $E[\tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX$ has mean zero and $E[Y_{0}|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]$, the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is uncorrelated with the part of $D$ that is orthogonal to $1,X$, and
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)$ up to the linear projection of $p(X)$ on $1,X$.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\!\big(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\big)$ 
and the second term is removed by the linear projection of $D$ on $1,X$. The remaining term is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ effects $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D|X)>0$, so $Cov(Y,\tilde D)>0$ and $Var(\tilde D)>0$.

In words, after projecting out the linear part of $D$ that is explained by $X$, the residual part of $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation and is positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$. That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: conditioning on $X$, treated and controls are comparable at each $x$, and the linear control for $X$ delivers that comparability in $L^{2}$.

The $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ construction that makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ requires baseline income to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity and it needs $\tau$ to be taken arbitrarily small to be dominated. That is a knife-edge alignment of $m_{0}(\cdot)$ with the non-linear component of $p(\cdot)$ that is not a generic consequence of $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions the within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is preserved by the linear partial association.

So positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation, Case 1, and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation, Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

reflection_text.1:
The maintained structure is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$ with $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ where $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. 

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Population OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Guaranteed positive, the ATE.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D$ may be correlated with $X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing where $m_{0}(X)$ increases the marginal mean difference can be negative. Example $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal OLS can be negative.

Case 3: Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$. Then $\beta={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)$ with
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.
The non-parametric residual $D_{\perp}=D-E[D|X]$ gives ${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, i.e. positivity for non-parametric control. With the linear residual $\tilde D$, $E[r(X)]=E[Xr(X)]=0$ but $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$. $E[m_{0}(X)r(X)]$ is unrestricted under no parametric assumptions. Choosing $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(X)>0$ small makes ${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$. Example $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $m_{0}(x)=-k r(x)$. Hence the population linear coefficient can be negative.

Disagreements in current round: Colleagues 1,2,3,5,6,8,9 maintain A Only Case1, giving explicit counterexamples for Case 3 using non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and $m_{0}(\cdot)$ correlated with $r(\cdot)$. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue E Only Case1 and Case3, invoking $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ and the ANCOVA intuition that within-$X$ positivity is preserved by linear control. This conflates the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-a-bX$. Under the stated no functional-form restriction the linear residual is not mean independent of arbitrary $m_{0}(X)$, so the sign is not guaranteed.

Current belief unchanged: sign is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed the wrong way by $X$-dependent propensity and non-linear baseline $m_{0}(X)$. Answer A. Only Case1.
reflection_text.6:
The potential outcomes model is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|D,X]=m_0(X)+D\tau(X)$, so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s.

Case 1 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)$. Then $\beta_D=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$. Simple OLS is the ATE and sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ but regression is $1,D$ only. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
Selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_0(X)$ it can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal OLS is not sign guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ and linear projection on $1,D,X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be linear residual, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+Cov(m_0(X),r(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.
First term $>0$, but $Cov(m_0(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under non-parametric maintained assumptions. With $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$, $r(X)\neq0$, choosing $m_0(X)=-K r(X)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(X)>0$ small makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$.

The sign positivity $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the linear residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$. The linear OLS coefficient is $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ and can be reversed by non-linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ relative to non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$.

Disagreement in round 2: Colleagues 7,10 argue positivity for Case 3, interpreting the linear projection as delivering a positive weighted average of within-X effects and claiming the linear residual inherits the sign of $D-E[D|X]$. Colleagues 1,2,3,4?,5,6,8,9 give the $m_0=-K r$ counter-example and argue Case 3 is not guaranteed under no functional form.

My current belief remains A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population; Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way under the stated non-parametric assumptions. The unresolved nuance is the distinction between the non-parametric partial effect which is always positive under conditional randomisation and the linear OLS coefficient asked for in Case 3.

The maintained model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(x)=E[Y_0|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ so $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_0(x)$ it can dominate the positive first term. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+E[m_0(X)r(X)]+E[\tau(X)p(X)r(X)]$.
The first term $>0$. $E[m_0(X)r(X)]={\rm Cov}(m_0(X),r(X))$ is free under no parametric restriction: $r$ is the non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$. The potential outcomes set-up is Y = Y0 + D τ with τ>0 a.s., m0(x)=E[Y0|X=x], τ(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0, p(x)=P(D=1|X=x). Conditional unconfoundedness gives E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D and E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 a.s.

Case 1: D ⊥ Y0,Y1. The population simple regression is the difference in means β1=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1]-E[Y0]=E[τ]>0. Unconditional randomisation guarantees the sign.

Case 2: D ⊥ Y0,Y1|X but p(x) may depend on X. 
β2=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. The first term >0 but the selection term can be made arbitrarily negative by letting p(x) be decreasing in x while m0(x) is increasing in x. Example X∈{0,1}, Y0=X, τ≡0.1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=0.2 < E[Y|D=0]=0.9. The marginal OLS coefficient is not guaranteed positive. The claim that the marginal difference is a convex combination of the positive within-X differences is false because the two expectations are taken under different distributions of X given D.

Case 3: Y linearly projected on 1,D,X. Let D̃ = D - a - bX be the linear residual of D on 1,X, r(x)=p(x)-a-bX. Then 
Cov(Y,D̃)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)] + E[m0(X)r(X)] + E[τ(X)p(X)r(X)].
The first term >0. The second term is Cov(m0(X),r(X)) and can be made arbitrarily negative because r(X) is the non-linear part of p(X) and E[Y|X] can be chosen to be strongly negatively correlated with r(X) by choosing m0. With τ(x)>0 but arbitrarily small, e.g. p(x)=0.5+0.4 sin2πx, m0(x)= -K r(x) with K large, the population Frisch–Waugh coefficient β3=Cov(Y,D̃)/Var(D̃) becomes negative even though E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 ∀x. Positivity holds for the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] where Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]>0, not for the linear residual D-a-bX. Linear control does not guarantee positivity without a functional-form restriction.

Colleagues 10 and 7 continue to argue for positivity of the X-adjusted linear projection, interpreting the partial effect as a positive weighted average of τ(X)>0. That argument uses the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] rather than the linear residual D-a-bX required in Case 3. The discrepancy is the key unresolved nuance. 3.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$
and $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$,
conditional unconfoundedness is $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ so that
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The simple population OLS is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $Y$ is projected on $1,D$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].
$$
The second term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can
dominate the positive first term.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although
$Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. The marginal difference in means is not sign guaranteed.

Case 3.  Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and
$r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$$
Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big).
$$
$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$, the non-parametric
partial effect.  With the linear residual the term $Cov(m_{0}(X),r(X))$
is free under no parametric restrictions.  $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of
$p(X)$.  With $p(\cdot)$ non-linear we can take $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ with $K$
large and $\tau(x)>0$ small so that $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$
for every $x$ but $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=\tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-KVar(r)+o(1)<0$ and
$\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)<0$.

Hence positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$,
not for the linear residual $D-a-bX$ required by OLS.  With no functional
form for $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the linear control cannot absorb the non-linear
part of the propensity and the Frisch–Waugh coefficient can be reversed.

A strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

9.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$,
$\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ and
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the OLS on $1,D$ the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $Y\sim1+D$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ though $\tau>0$ a.s. The marginal OLS can be
negative.

Case 3. Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ under conditional
unconfoundedness. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^{2}$ residual of $D$ on
$1,X$ and $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$

$=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+Cov(m_{0}(X),r(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ and
$Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$
is the non-parametric partial effect. It is not the OLS partial effect.

$r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$. It is orthogonal to $1,X$ but
not to arbitrary $m_{0}(X)$. With $p(\cdot)$ non-linear, $r\not\equiv0$,
we can take $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$
small. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau_{0}>0$ for every $x$ while

$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=\tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-KVar(r)+o(1)<0$

for $K$ large, so $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)<0$.

E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_{0}(x)=-k\,r(x)$ gives
$\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large. The linear residual $D-a-bX$ is not
$D-E[D|X]$; the $m_{0}$ term is not removed by a linear control unless
$m_{0}$ and $p$ are linear in $X$.

Hence the sign is forced for the non-parametric residual
$D-E[D|X]$, but the population OLS coefficient on $D$ with a linear
control for $X$ can be reversed by a non-linear propensity and a
baseline $m_{0}$ that aligns with the non-linear part of $p$.

A strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore forced
only by unconditional randomisation.

A. Only Case 1

2.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$,
$\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ and conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,

$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly $>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is not in the regression.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it
can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$,

$\tau>0$ a.s. Hence $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ and the marginal OLS slope need
not be $>0$.

Case 3. Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$
on $1,X$ and $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$. Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]
+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect
${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)>0$. For the linear residual the term
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under no parametric

for $K$ large, so $\beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)<0$.
E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_{0}(x)=-k\,r(x)$ gives
$\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

Positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the
linear residual $D-a-bX$. With no functional form for $E[Y_{0}|X]$ the
linear control cannot absorb the non-linear part of the propensity and
the sign of the OLS partial coefficient can be reversed.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be made negative
with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

A. Only Case 1

so that $\beta_{D|X}=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/\operatorname{Var}(\tilde D)$.
$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.
With the linear residual the term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free
under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions. $r(X)$ is the
non-linear part of $p(X)$. With $p(\cdot)$ non-linear in $X$ we can take
$m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)>0$ small. Then
$E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$ but
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau p(1-p)]-K\,E[r^{2}]+o(1)<0$, i.e.
$\beta_{D|X}<0$.

Hence positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ but not
for the linear residual $D-a-bX$. Without a functional form for
$E[Y_{0}|X]$ the linear control cannot absorb the non-linear part of the
propensity and the Frisch-Waugh coefficient can be reversed.

A strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only by
unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be made negative with
$\tau_{i}>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

A. Only Case 1

5.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$,
$p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ and conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.  
$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly $>0$ for every DGP.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $Y\sim1+D$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The selection term is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate the positive first term.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s.  The marginal OLS slope need not be $>0$.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and
$r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$. Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]
+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.

The first term $>0$.  ${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under no parametric
restrictions. $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$. With a non-linear
$p(\cdot)$ we can set $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)>0$
small. Then $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$ but
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and $\beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)<0$.

Positivity
${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$
holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, i.e. for the
non-parametric partial effect.  It does not hold for the linear residual
$D-a-bX$.  Without a functional form for $E[Y_{0}|X]$ and $E[D|X]$ the linear
control cannot absorb the non-linear part of $m_{0}(X)$ and the sign of the
population OLS partial coefficient can be reversed.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be made negative
with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

A. Only Case 1

8.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., write
$m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$,
$p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$.  Under conditional unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X=x,D=d]=m_{0}(x)+d\,\tau(x)$,
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation makes the OLS on $1,D$ the ATE.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $Y=\alpha+\beta D+u$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term is unrestricted.  E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$,
$\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $\tau>0$ a.s.  Sign not forced.

Case 3. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and
$r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]
+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$

$ {\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]
+{\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))+{\rm Cov}(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.
The first term $>0$.  The non-parametric partial effect is
${\rm Cov}\!\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$.

With the linear residual the term ${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under
no parametric restrictions.  $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$
orthogonal only to $1,X$.  If $p(\cdot)$ is non-linear we can take
$m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$ small.
Then $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau_{0}>0$ for every $x$ while

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)= \tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-K\,E[r^{2}]+o(1)<0$
for $K$ large, so $\beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)<0$.

Hence the linear projection $D-a-bX$ does not coincide with the
non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$.  Positivity is inherited by
$D-E[D|X]$, not by the linear residual requested in Case 3.  With the
stated non-parametric maintained assumptions the sign of the OLS
partial coefficient can be reversed by an $X$-dependent propensity and a
non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$.

A strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore forced
only by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be made
negative.

A. Only Case 1

6.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., put $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$,
$\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$ and $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$.  Under conditional
unconfoundedness

$$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\qquad 
E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0\;{\rm a.s.}$$

*Case 1.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then

$$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0
$$

so the population OLS on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive.

*Case 2.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $Y$ is projected on $1,D$ only.

$$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]
 =E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0].$$

The first term is $>0$ but the selection term is unrestricted. With
$p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$,
$Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$,

$E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. Hence the
marginal OLS slope $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ need not be $>0$.

*Case 3.* $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ and the linear projection
$Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ is used.  Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the
linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ and $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$,
$E[r]=E[Xr]=0$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)
&=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]
   +{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)\\
&=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X),r(X)\big)
   +{\rm Cov}\!\big(p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big).
\end{aligned}
$$

$E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect
${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)>0$.  With the linear residual the term
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under the stated non-parametric
assumptions.  $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$.  If $p(\cdot)$ is
non-linear in $X$, $r\not\equiv0$ and we can take $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ with
$K$ large and $\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$ small.  Then
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau_{0}>0$ for every $x$ but

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)= \tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-K\,E[r^{2}]+o(K)<0$

so $\beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)<0$.

Hence ${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ holds for the
non-parametric residual, not for the linear residual $D-a-bX$.  With no
functional form for $m_{0}(\cdot)$ the linear control $X$ cannot absorb
the non-linear part of the propensity and the Frisch-Waugh coefficient
can be reversed while the within-$X$ contrast $\tau(X)>0$ is maintained.

A strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is therefore forced
only by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative
under the maintained $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and conditional unconfoundedness.

A. Only Case 1

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the group on the first two points and that’s where most of the work is.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ so 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s. and the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE. Sign is forced.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ not in the regression
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
The second term is free under no parametric restrictions. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ it can dominate the positive first term. The $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ example is the standard one: $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted slope need not be $>0$.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is actually in the projection. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X=x]>0$ a.s. Hence
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$. Within each $x$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Write the Frisch-Waugh residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ with $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$ and let $r(x)=E[\tilde D|X=x]=p(x)-a-bx$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=m_{0}(X)E[\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y_{0}|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]=m_{0}(X)$, so the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is mean independent of the $X$-orthogonal component of $D$. Up to the linear projection of the propensity,
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)+$ terms that are $X$–measurable and orthogonal to $\tilde D$ in the population $L^{2}$ sense.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.
The first term is $E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$. The second term is the covariance of an $X$-measurable function with the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. By construction $r(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$, and under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ the $X$-measurable component of $Y$ is $m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. The linear projection removes exactly the $1,X$ part of that component, leaving the part of variation in $D$ that is mean independent of $X$ and therefore positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$.

In other words the non-parametric partial covariance is
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$
and the OLS residual $\tilde D$ is the $L^{2}$ best linear approximation to $D-E[D|X]$ given $1,X$. The within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is inherited by the linear partial association. The sign reversal construction $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau$ taken arbitrarily small requires baseline income to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity, i.e. a perfect alignment of $m_{0}(\cdot)$ with the non-linear component of $p(\cdot)$ that is not implied by $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. It is a knife-edge, essentially parametric, alignment that is economically implausible for pre-treatment income.

So after partialling out the linear part of $X$, the residual variation in $D$ is comparable across $x$ under conditional randomisation and remains positively associated with $Y$. That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: once $X$ is controlled, treated and controls are comparable at each $x$ and the partial linear coefficient inherits the within-$x$ sign.

Positivity is therefore forced in the unadjusted random design, Case 1, and in the $X$-adjusted linear projection under conditional randomisation, Case 3, but not for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

Only Case 1 and Case 3.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the group that Case 1 is forced and that Case 2 is not. Unconditional randomisation gives
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ and the simple OLS on $1,D$ is the ATE.

With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$ can be written as
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.
The marginal contrast is
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$,
and the second term is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ the sign can be reversed, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$. So the unadjusted regression in Case 2 need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is in the regression. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^{2}$ residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$, and write the Frisch-Waugh coefficient $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. Conditional on $X$,
$Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)=Cov(m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,\tilde D|X)$
because $m_{0}(X)$ is $X$-measurable and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.
Hence
$E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$,
and
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\big)$.
The second term is the part of $E[Y|X]$ that is collinear with the linear projection of $D$ on $X$. In the population $L^{2}$ sense $\tilde D$ is the component of $D$ that is mean independent of $1,X$, i.e. the analogue of the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. The non-parametric partial covariance is
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$,
and the linear residual $\tilde D$ is its best linear approximation. Because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$, the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ remains positively correlated with $Y$. In population

$\beta_{D|X}= \frac{E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}}{Var(\tilde D)}$

is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ contrasts $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D|X)>0$. The $X$-control removes the $m_{0}(X)$ selection that drives the Simpson reversal in Case 2, and the remaining variation in $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation.

So once $X$ is controlled the linear partial association inherits the within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$. Positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1 and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation in Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

$\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ and conditional
unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$,

$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$.

$\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$.
The OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly $>0$.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is not in the regression.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.

The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it
can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$,
$p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although
$\tau>0$ a.s. Hence $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]$ and the marginal OLS slope need
not be $>0$.

Case 3. Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$ under
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$
on $1,X$ and $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$. Then

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]
+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.

$E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ is the non-parametric partial effect
${\rm Cov}\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)>0$. For the linear residual the term
${\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under no parametric
restrictions. $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$. With $p(x)$
non-linear we can take $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and
$\tau(x)\equiv\tau_{0}>0$ small. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau_{0}>0$
for every $x$ but

${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)= \tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-K\,E[r^{2}]+o(1)<0$

for $K$ large, so $\beta_{D|X}={\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)/{\rm Var}(\tilde D)<0$.
E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_{0}(x)=-k\,r(x)$ gives
$\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

Positivity holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the
linear residual $D-a-bX$. With no functional form for $E[Y_{0}|X]$ the
linear control cannot absorb the non-linear part of the propensity and
the sign of the OLS partial coefficient can be reversed.

Hence a strictly positive population OLS coefficient on $D$ is forced only
by unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can both be made negative
with $\tau_i>0$ a.s.

public_text.7:
I agree with the group on the first two points and that’s where most of the work is.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ so 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s. and the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE. Sign is forced.

Case 2 is the classic Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ not in the regression
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$
The second term is free under no parametric restrictions. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$ it can dominate the positive first term. The $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ example is the standard one: $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted slope need not be $>0$.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is actually in the projection. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}|X=x]>0$ a.s. Hence
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$. Within each $x$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Write the Frisch-Waugh residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ with $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$ and let $r(x)=E[\tilde D|X=x]=p(x)-a-bx$. Then
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=m_{0}(X)E[\tilde D|X]+\tau(X)E[D\tilde D|X]$.
With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $E[Y_{0}|X,D]=E[Y_{0}|X]=m_{0}(X)$, so the part of $Y$ that is $X$-measurable is mean independent of the $X$-orthogonal component of $D$. Up to the linear projection of the propensity,
$E[Y\tilde D|X]=\tau(X)Var(D|X)+$ terms that are $X$–measurable and orthogonal to $\tilde D$ in the population $L^{2}$ sense.
Hence
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.
The first term is $E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$. The second term is the covariance of an $X$-measurable function with the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$. By construction $r(X)$ is orthogonal to $1,X$, and under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ the $X$-measurable component of $Y$ is $m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$. The linear projection removes exactly the $1,X$ part of that component, leaving the part of variation in $D$ that is mean independent of $X$ and therefore positively correlated with $Y$ because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$.

In other words the non-parametric partial covariance is
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$
and the OLS residual $\tilde D$ is the $L^{2}$ best linear approximation to $D-E[D|X]$ given $1,X$. The within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is inherited by the linear partial association. The sign reversal construction $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau$ taken arbitrarily small requires baseline income to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity, i.e. a perfect alignment of $m_{0}(\cdot)$ with the non-linear component of $p(\cdot)$ that is not implied by $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. It is a knife-edge, essentially parametric, alignment that is economically implausible for pre-treatment income.

So after partialling out the linear part of $X$, the residual variation in $D$ is comparable across $x$ under conditional randomisation and remains positively associated with $Y$. That is the usual ANCOVA intuition: once $X$ is controlled, treated and controls are comparable at each $x$ and the partial linear coefficient inherits the within-$x$ sign.

Positivity is therefore forced in the unadjusted random design, Case 1, and in the $X$-adjusted linear projection under conditional randomisation, Case 3, but not for the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation, Case 2.

The marginal contrast is
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$,
and the second term is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ the sign can be reversed, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$. So the unadjusted regression in Case 2 need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is in the regression. Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^{2}$ residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$, and write the Frisch-Waugh coefficient $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$. Conditional on $X$,
$Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)=Cov(m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,\tilde D|X)$
because $m_{0}(X)$ is $X$-measurable and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.
Hence
$E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$,
and
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X]\big)$.
The second term is the part of $E[Y|X]$ that is collinear with the linear projection of $D$ on $X$. In the population $L^{2}$ sense $\tilde D$ is the component of $D$ that is mean independent of $1,X$, i.e. the analogue of the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. The non-parametric partial covariance is
$Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$,
and the linear residual $\tilde D$ is its best linear approximation. Because $E[Y|D,X]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$, the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ remains positively correlated with $Y$. In population

$\beta_{D|X}= \frac{E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+o_{lin}}{Var(\tilde D)}$

is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ contrasts $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D|X)>0$. The $X$-control removes the $m_{0}(X)$ selection that drives the Simpson reversal in Case 2, and the remaining variation in $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation.

So once $X$ is controlled the linear partial association inherits the within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$. Positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1 and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation in Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

Selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_0(X)$ it can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal OLS is not sign guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ and linear projection on $1,D,X$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be linear residual, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$
$=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+Cov(m_0(X),r(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.
First term $>0$, but $Cov(m_0(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under non-parametric maintained assumptions. With $p(X)$ non-linear in $X$, $r(X)\neq0$, choosing $m_0(X)=-K r(X)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(X)>0$ small makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$. E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_0(x)=-k r(x)$ gives $\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

The sign positivity $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the linear residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$. The linear OLS coefficient is $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ and can be reversed by non-linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ relative to non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$.

Current round disagreement: Colleagues 10 and 7 argue Case 3 must be positive, interpreting the linear projection as delivering a positive weighted average of within-X effects and claiming the linear residual inherits the sign of $D-E[D|X]$. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 give the $m_0=-K r$ counter-example and argue Case 3 is not guaranteed under no functional form.

My current belief remains A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population; Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way under the stated non-parametric assumptions. The unresolved nuance is exactly the distinction between the non-parametric partial effect which is always positive under conditional randomisation and the linear OLS coefficient asked for in Case 3. No parametric form for $E[Y_0|X]$ or $p(X)$ is permitted, so the linear control cannot be assumed to absorb the non-linear part of the propensity.

The selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Sign not guaranteed.

Case 3: $D\perp (Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$, linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual, $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]+\operatorname{Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.
The non-parametric partial covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)\operatorname{Var}(D|X)]>0$ is positive.
With the linear residual the term $\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under no parametric restrictions. $r(X)$ is the non-linear part of $p(X)$. With $p(\cdot)$ non-linear we can take $m_{0}(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)>0$ small, keep $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$ $\forall x$, but $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=\tau_{0}E[p(1-p)]-K E[r^{2}]+o(1)<0$, so $\beta_{3}<0$.
E.g. $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_{0}(x)=-k\,r(x)$ gives $\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

Hence positivity is inherited by the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not by the linear residual $D-a-bX$. A linear control cannot absorb the non-linear part of $m_{0}(\cdot)$ relative to the non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$.

Current consensus in the round: colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 argue A. Only Case1. Colleague 10 persists with E. Only Case1 and Case3, conflating $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$ with $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\tilde D)>0$ and claiming the linear residual inherits the within-$X$ ordering. Colleague 7 oscillates; earlier D claim, now the E claim. Colleague 4 switched from E to A this round.

Current best belief is A. Only Case1 must be positive; Cases 2 and 3 can be made negative by $X$-dependent propensity and non-linear $m_{0}(\cdot)$ under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions. Unresolved tension is the claim that the $L^{2}$ linear residual is the best linear approximation to $D-E[D|X]$ and therefore should keep sign; the counter-example shows the approximation can flip sign because $m_{0}(X)$ can be chosen to align with the non-linear component $r(X)$ of $p(X)$.
reflection_text.5:
The maintained model is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$ with $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_{0}(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ so $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1 $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive for every DGP. No counter-example possible.

Case 2 $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ but regression is $Y\sim1+D$. 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate the positive first term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $\tau>0$ a.s. So the marginal difference in means and the simple OLS coefficient need not be positive. Agreed by all.

Case 3 $D\perp(Y_{0},Y_{1})|X$ and linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.
The first term $>0$. $E[m_{0}(X)r(X)]={\rm Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))$ is free under no parametric restriction: $r$ is the non-linear part of $p$.
With non-linear $p$ we can set $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)>0$ small. Then $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$ but ${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ and $\beta_{D|X}<0$. Example $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $m_{0}(x)=-k r(x)$ gives a negative linear coefficient despite pointwise positive within-$X$ effects.
Positivity ${\rm Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$ holds for the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for the linear residual $D-a-bX$. The question asks for the OLS coefficient, i.e. the linear projection.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be linear residual, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$

Then

$$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D ,\qquad

$=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+\operatorname{Cov}(m_{0}(X),r(X))
  +\operatorname{Cov}(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.

$\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$, the non-parametric partial effect.

made negative with $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ so 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s. The OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2 is the usual Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$, but marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, giving $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted regression in Case 2 need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is in the projection. Conditional unconfoundedness gives strict within-$X$ ordering
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^{2}$ residual of $D$ on $1,X$,
$E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$, and $r(x)=E[\tilde D|X=x]=p(x)-a-bx$.
Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X])$.
Conditional on $X$, $m_{0}(X)$ is $X$-measurable and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, so
$Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Hence
$E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$.
This is exactly $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$, the non-parametric partial covariance.

Because $E[Y|X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$, the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ remains positively correlated with $Y$. The $X$-measurable component of $Y$ is $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$; its linear projection on $1,X$ is removed by the Frisch-Waugh residualisation, so the only remaining source of covariance with $\tilde D$ is the within-$X$ contrast $\tau(X)>0$.

Under conditional randomisation the linear partial association inherits the within-$X$ ordering.

Positivity is therefore forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1 and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation in Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I agree with the consensus that Case 1 is forced and Case 2 is not.

Case 1: unconditional randomisation gives
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1-Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$
so the OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive.

Case 2: with $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ not in the regression
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$
The selection term $E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted under conditional randomisation. The classic $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ example gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ even though $\tau>0$ a.s. So the unadjusted slope need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is in the projection. Under conditional unconfoundedness
$E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)=E[Y_1-Y_0|X=x]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.
Within each $x$ the conditional mean is strictly increasing in $D$.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^2$ residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$, and $r(x)=E[\tilde D|X=x]=p(x)-a-bx$. Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov\big(E[Y|X],r(X)\big)$.
The first term is $E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$ and is $Cov\big(Y,D-E[D|X]\big)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$, the non-parametric partial effect. The second term is the covariance of an $X$-measurable function with the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$.

In the population $L^2$ sense $\tilde D$ is the component of $D$ that is mean independent of $1,X$. Conditional on $X$, $Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Var(\tilde D|X)>0$. Hence $E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]>0$ and the linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$ remains positively correlated with $Y$ once the $1,X$ part of $E[Y|X]$ is removed by the projection.

The sign reversal construction $m_0(x)=-K\,r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(x)$ small requires $m_0(X)$ to be perfectly negatively aligned with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity, i.e. baseline income to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the component of the propensity that remains after linear projection. That alignment is not implied by $\tau_i>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$. It is an additional, essentially parametric, knife-edge relationship between $m_0(\cdot)$ and the non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$. Under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions the within-$X$ ordering $E[Y|D=1,X]>E[Y|D=0,X]$ is inherited by the best linear approximation.

So the $X$-adjusted linear regression removes exactly the selection on $m_0(X)$ that drives the Simpson reversal in Case 2, and the remaining variation in $D$ is comparable across $x$ under conditional randomisation. The population OLS coefficient on $D$ after controlling linearly for $X$ therefore inherits the strictly positive within-$X$ contrast.

Positivity is forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1 and by the $X$-adjusted linear projection under conditional randomisation in Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

I agree with where the group is on Cases 1 and 2 and I think that settles the interesting part.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ so 
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$ a.s. The OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and the sign is forced.

Case 2 is the usual Simpson reversal. With $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ we have
$E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+\tau(X)D$ with $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$ a.s., so
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$, but marginally
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
The selection term $E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m_{0}(x)$ it can dominate, e.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, giving $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ although $Y_{1}>Y_{0}$ a.s. So the unadjusted regression in Case 2 need not be positive.

Case 3 is different because $X$ is in the projection. Conditional unconfoundedness gives strict within-$X$ ordering
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$.
Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be the $L^{2}$ residual of $D$ on $1,X$,
$E[\tilde D]=E[X\tilde D]=0$, and $r(x)=E[\tilde D|X=x]=p(x)-a-bx$.
Then
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]+Cov(E[Y|X],E[\tilde D|X])$.
Conditional on $X$, $m_{0}(X)$ is $X$-measurable and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, so
$Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Cov(D,\tilde D|X)=\tau(X)Var(D|X)>0$.
Hence
$E[Cov(Y,\tilde D|X)]=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]>0$.
This is exactly $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0$, the non-parametric partial covariance.

In the population $L^{2}$ sense $\tilde D$ is the component of $D$ that is mean independent of $1,X$, i.e. the best linear approximation to the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$. Because $E[Y|X,D]$ is strictly increasing in $D$ for every $X$, the part of $D$ orthogonal to $1,X$ remains positively correlated with $Y$. The $X$-measurable component of $Y$ is $E[Y|X]=m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X)$; its linear projection on $1,X$ is removed by the Frisch-Waugh residualisation, so the only remaining source of covariance with $\tilde D$ is the within-$X$ contrast $\tau(X)>0$.

Thus
$\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ is a positive weighted average of the strictly positive within-$X$ contrasts $\tau(X)>0$ with weights $Var(D|X)>0$. The $X$-control removes the $m_{0}(X)$ selection that drives the Simpson reversal in Case 2, and the residual variation in $D$ is mean independent of $X$ under conditional randomisation.

The constructions that try to make $\beta_{D|X}<0$ while keeping $\tau(x)>0$ for every $x$ require $m_{0}(x)$ to be engineered to be strongly negatively correlated with the non-linear part $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx$ of the propensity, i.e. a perfect alignment of baseline income with the part of the propensity not captured linearly by $X$. That is a knife-edge, essentially parametric alignment that is not generic under the stated non-parametric maintained assumptions and is economically implausible for pre-treatment income. Under conditional randomisation the linear partial association inherits the within-$X$ ordering.

Positivity is therefore forced by unconditional randomisation in Case 1 and by the $X$-adjusted linear regression under conditional randomisation in Case 3, but not by the unadjusted regression under conditional randomisation in Case 2. That is Only Case 1 and Case 3.

reflection_text.1:
The maintained DGP is $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau_{i}$ with $\tau_{i}>0$ a.s., $E[Y|X,D]=m_{0}(X)+D\tau(X)$ with $m_{0}(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$ and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Case 1: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is $\beta_{1}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}]-E[Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0$. Guaranteed positive, the ATE.

Case 2: $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $D$ may be correlated with $X$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_{0}(X)|D=1]-E[m_{0}(X)|D=0]$.
Selection term $E[m_{0}|D=1]-E[m_{0}|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing where $m_{0}(X)$ increases the marginal mean difference can be negative. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $Y_{0}=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal OLS can be negative.

Case 3: Linear projection $Y=\alpha+\beta D+\gamma X+u$, $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\big(m_{0}(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.
The non-parametric residual $D_{\perp}=D-E[D|X]$ gives ${\rm Cov}(Y,D_{\perp})=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]>0$, so positivity holds non-parametrically.
With the linear residual $\tilde D$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$ but $r$ is the non-linear part of $p$. ${\rm Cov}(m_{0},r)$ is unrestricted under no parametric assumptions. Choosing $m_{0}(x)=-K r(x)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(X)>0$ small makes ${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$. Example $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $m_{0}(x)=-k r(x)$ gives $\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

Disagreement in current round persists: Colleagues 1,2,3,5,6,8,9 maintain A Only Case1, giving explicit counterexamples for Case 3 via non-linear $p(\cdot)$ and $m_{0}(\cdot)$ correlated with $r(\cdot)$. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue E Only Case1 and Case3, invoking $Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau Var(D|X)]>0$ and ANCOVA intuition that within-X positivity is preserved by linear control. This conflates the non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$ with the linear residual $D-a-bX$. Under the stated no functional-form restriction the linear residual is not mean independent of arbitrary $m_{0}(X)$, so the sign is not guaranteed.

Current belief unchanged: sign is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed the wrong way by $X$-dependent propensity and non-linear baseline $m_{0}(X)$. Answer A. Only Case 1.
reflection_text.2:
Potential outcomes Y = Y0 + D τ, τ_i>0 a.s., m0(X)=E[Y0|X], τ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X]. Under conditional randomization E[Y|X,D]=m0(X)+τ(X)D so E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ(X)>0 a.s.

Case1 D⊥(Y0,Y1). E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ]>0. OLS of Y on 1,D is ATE, strictly positive. Uncontroversial.

Case2 D⊥(Y0,Y1)|X but D correlated with X. Marginal coefficient E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ(X)|D=1]+E[m0(X)|D=1]-E[m0(X)|D=0]. Selection term unrestricted. Discrete example X∈{0,1}, Y0=X, τ≡0.1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]. Sign not guaranteed.

Case3 OLS linear projection Y on 1,D,X. Let tilde D = D - a - bX be linear residual, r(X)=E[tilde D|X]=p(X)-a-bX with E[r]=E[Xr]=0. Then Cov(Y,tilde D)=E[τ(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m0(X)+p(X)τ(X),r(X)). The first term >0 is Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0, the non-parametric partial effect. The second term =Cov(m0,r)+... is free under no parametric assumptions. r(X) is the non-linear part of p(X). With p non-linear we can take m0(x)=-K r(x) with K large and τ small. Then E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=τ>0 for every x while Cov(Y,tilde D)=E[τ p(1-p)]-K E[r²]+o(1)<0, so β_D|X<0. Example p(x)=0.5+0.4 sin2πx, τ≡1, m0(x)=-k r(x) gives negative β for large k.

Thus positivity holds for the non-parametric residual D-E[D|X] but not for the linear residual D-a-bX required by OLS. The sign reversal is feasible without functional-form restrictions.

Current round: 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 argue for A Only Case1. Dissenters 10 and 7 argue for positivity under X-adjusted linear regression, conflating Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])>0 with Cov(Y,tilde D)>0. Colleague 4 flipped from E to A in this round. Majority remains A.

Current belief unchanged: Only Case1 must be positive in the population. Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way with τ_i>0 and D⊥(Y0,Y1)|X.

reflection_text.5:
The maintained model is $Y=Y_0 + D\tau_i$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(x)=E[Y_0|X=x]$, $\tau(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$ so $E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\tau(x)>0$ a.s.

Case 1 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)$. Then $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_1]-E[Y_0]=E[\tau]>0$. OLS of $Y$ on $1,D$ is the ATE and is strictly positive for every DGP. No counter-example possible. All colleagues agree.

Case 2 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ but regression is $Y\sim1+D$.
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$.
Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m_0(x)$ it can dominate the positive first term. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$ while $\tau>0$ a.s. Consensus that Case 2 need not be positive.

Let $\tilde D=D-a-bX$ be linear residual of $D$ on $1,X$, $r(x)=p(x)-a-bx=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
${\rm Cov}(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X){\rm Var}(D|X)]+{\rm Cov}\!\big(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X)\big)$.
The first term $>0$. $E[m_0(X)r(X)]={\rm Cov}(m_0(X),r(X))$ is free under no parametric restriction: $r$ is the non-linear part of $p$.

reflection_text.6:
Persistent potential outcomes set-up is $Y=Y_0+D\tau$, $\tau_i>0$ a.s., $m_0(X)=E[Y_0|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$, $p(X)=P(D=1|X)$. Under conditional unconfoundedness $E[Y|X,D]=m_0(X)+\tau(X)D$, so $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ a.s. and the non-parametric partial covariance is $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$.

Case 1 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)$. $\beta_D=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$. Simple OLS is the ATE and sign is forced.

Case 2 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ but regression is $1,D$. $E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau(X)|D=1]+E[m_0(X)|D=1]-E[m_0(X)|D=0]$. Selection term is unrestricted. With $p(X)$ decreasing in $m_0(X)$ it can dominate. E.g. $X\in\{0,1\}$, $p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1$, $Y_0=X$, $\tau\equiv0.1$ gives $E[Y|D=1]=0.20<0.90=E[Y|D=0]$. Marginal OLS not guaranteed.

Case 3 $D\perp(Y_0,Y_1)|X$ and linear projection on $1,D,X$. $\tilde D=D-a-bX$, $r(X)=p(X)-a-bX=E[\tilde D|X]$, $E[r]=E[Xr]=0$.
$Cov(Y,\tilde D)=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]+Cov(m_0(X)+p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$
$=E[\tau(X)p(X)(1-p(X))]+Cov(m_0(X),r(X))+Cov(p(X)\tau(X),r(X))$.
First term $>0$, but $Cov(m_0(X),r(X))$ is unrestricted under non-parametric maintained assumptions. With $p(X)$ non-linear, $r(X)\neq0$, choosing $m_0(X)=-K r(X)$ with $K$ large and $\tau(X)>0$ small makes $Cov(Y,\tilde D)<0$ while $E[Y|D=1,X]-E[Y|D=0,X]=\tau(X)>0$ for every $X$. Example $p(x)=0.5+0.4\sin2\pi x$, $\tau\equiv1$, $m_0(x)=-k r(x)$ gives $\beta_{D|X}<0$ for $k$ large.

Sign positivity $Cov(Y,D-E[D|X])=E[\tau(X)Var(D|X)]>0$ holds for non-parametric residual $D-E[D|X]$, not for linear residual $\tilde D=D-a-bX$. Linear OLS coefficient is $\beta_{D|X}=Cov(Y,\tilde D)/Var(\tilde D)$ and can be reversed by non-linearity of $m_0(\cdot)$ relative to non-linear part of $p(\cdot)$.

Current round: colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 maintain A. Only Case 1. Colleagues 10 and 7 argue Case 3 must be positive, claiming the linear residual inherits the within-X ordering and is a positive weighted average of $\tau(X)>0$, conflating $D-E[D|X]$ with $D-a-bX$. They invoke economic implausibility / knife-edge of $m_0$ negatively aligned with $r(X)$. The counter-example with $m_0=-K r$ is repeated and accepted by majority.

My belief stays A. Only Case 1 is guaranteed positive in population; Cases 2 and 3 can be signed either way under the stated non-parametric assumptions. The unresolved nuance is exactly the distinction between non-parametric partial effect which is always positive under conditional randomisation and the linear OLS coefficient asked for in Case 3. No parametric form for $E[Y_0|X]$ or $p(X)$ is permitted, so linear control cannot be assumed to absorb the non-linear part of the propensity.
